title: Frost in the Meadow and Mustangs on the Hill
summary: Two days of drone flying in early November: a snowy meadow near Blue Lakes, California, at 17°F, still open but soon to close for the season, and a hillside on the outskirts of Carson City, Nevada, where wild mustangs grazed. The meadow's frosted pines and winding creek open the Note.

post.title: Seventeen degrees and wild mustangs
post.body:
November 4 and 5 were two days of flying my drone in two very different places, on two mornings at about the same time.

## Seventeen degrees at Blue Lakes

The first, on November 4, was a meadow near Blue Lakes, California, on public land. It's still open for now, but it will close soon for the snow. It was 17°F while I was flying. At 7:31 in the morning the sky was a deep, clean blue, the ridgeline was white end to end, and every pine around the meadow was frosted. From above, the creek is the thing that holds the picture together: one dark line curling through the snow and brush, with the forest climbing toward the peaks on the right.

I'm glad I went when I did. A place like this only gives you a short window before the snow shuts it until spring, and that morning felt like the last good look at it for a while.

> From above, the creek is the thing that holds the picture together: one dark line curling through the snow and brush, with the forest climbing toward the peaks on the right.

## Mustangs outside Carson City

The second location, the next morning, November 5, was near Carson City, Nevada, where wild mustangs live on the hillsides on the outskirts of the city. Same season, same cold, but a completely different subject: open desert slopes and horses instead of a frozen creek and pines. I kept a comfortable distance from the horses the whole time, far enough that they didn't react. I pushed in a little, then pulled back away and left them to it.

Everything here was flown where it's allowed and done by the rules.

## Go now

What I learned: when a place is about to close for the season, go now. The cold is part of the picture.

episode.title: Seventeen degrees
episode.script:
Narrated by Starlee.

Seven thirty in the morning, the fourth of November, and the thermometer said seventeen degrees.

Christian was up in a meadow near Blue Lakes, California, on public land. It was still open, but not for long. The snow would close it soon. He wasn't there to ride or hike. He was there to fly his drone.

From the air, the whole place opened up. The sky was that deep, clean blue you only get on a cold, clear morning. A long ridge of mountains stood white from one end to the other. Closer in, every pine was frosted, as if someone had gone over the forest with a dusting brush.

And down in the middle of the meadow, a creek ran dark through the snow, curling back on itself the way creeks do when they are in no hurry at all.

***

Here's what I like about that picture. There's a lot of white in it, and a lot of trees. It would be easy to get lost. But Christian put that one dark ribbon of water right where the eye wants to land, and the rest of the scene arranges itself around it. Finding the line that holds a picture together is the whole job, and he found it at seventeen degrees.

He also chose the moment. A meadow about to close for the season gives you a short window, and he took it.

***

The next morning, the fifth of November, at about the same hour, the second location could hardly have been more different. On the outskirts of Carson City, Nevada, the hillsides belong in part to wild mustangs. Same cold season, a different country altogether: open desert slopes, and horses that answer to no one.

Christian kept a comfortable distance from them the whole time, far enough that they didn't react. He eased in a little, then pulled back away and let them be. Knowing when to back off is part of the craft too.

All of it, the meadow and the mustangs, was flown where flying is allowed, and done by the rules.

Two mornings, two places, one sky.

Some seasons end quietly. This one, he caught on the way out.
